lines: Thunder shook rings across the cauldron water, but everyone near me is still standing.
I checked the roof after the first lightning strike. Water was already running toward the hides.
The bell sounded tiny under that sky, though we all heard it.
Every buckle on the wall rattled when the thunder rolled over us.
I moved the drying racks away from the windows before the rain came through.
One of the horses broke its lead in fright. We found it behind the smithy.
The children counted the seconds after each flash until the storm passed.
A leak opened above my workbench, but the finished saddles stayed dry.
I have never seen the village square empty so quickly.
We kept the doors open for anyone caught away from home.
The storm split an old tree beside the tannery without touching the roof.
Wet hides can be saved. A neighbor under a falling branch cannot.
I gave out every spare cloak I had while people checked the fields.
The air smelled scorched long after the lightning moved away.
No one slept much while the shutters kept banging.
I need to replace three straps the frightened animals tore loose.
Next time, the emergency lanterns should be somewhere easier to reach.
We found one goat under the drying racks after dawn.
The rain exposed a weak patch in the workshop roof.
The sky is quiet now, but my hands still expect another crack of thunder.
I checked dry hides and dye racks for sparks first, then checked faces for smoke and <dark_gray><wavy>fear</wavy></dark_gray>.
We passed water hand to hand and kept people away from the smoke.
The hides can wait. People come first.
A spark reached the drying room before anyone smelled it.
I dragged two burning racks into the street and lost my apron doing it.
Smoke found every crack the rain never could.
Someone broke the tannery window so we could reach the back room.
The water ruined a week of dyeing, but it stopped the flames.
We wrapped the worst burns in clean cloth until the cleric arrived.
My tools are black with soot, and I am glad that is the worst of it.
The leather fed the fire faster than I care to remember.
We formed a line from the well before the bell finished ringing.
A child spotted the smoke and shouted before any adult did.
I keep checking the walls for heat even though the fire is out.
The animals panicked at the smell. Half the village helped catch them.
We need covered water barrels near every workshop.
Nothing in that room was worth going back through the flames alone.
The cauldron cracked when cold water hit it.
I salvaged a few tools after dawn. Everything else can be replaced.
Today the whole village smells of wet ash.
During a raid, the hides can soak another day. Who makes it behind a door matters more.
The horns stopped, but my hands still expect another wave from the road.
We counted living neighbors before saddles, tools, or emeralds.
Raiders found the tannery door barred and three angry villagers behind it.
I cut harness straps loose so the animals could reach shelter faster.
A crossbow bolt went through the drying rack beside my head.
The bell gave us enough warning to get the children indoors.
I saw a farmer hold the lane with nothing but an axe and nerve.
We used rolled hides against the windows until the fighting moved on.
One saddle took a bolt that might have found its rider.
The workshop floor became a place for bandages before the raid ended.
I can replace stolen leather. I cannot replace the neighbors we lost.
Someone kept the east gate clear when panic could have blocked it.
The pillagers cut every lead they could reach. We are still finding animals.
I spent the last wave carrying water instead of a weapon.
Our outer fences need stronger gates before another horn sounds.
The raiders knew where our supplies were. We should spread them out.
I have three torn shields waiting for new straps.
Everyone who fought came home with gear needing work.
The village held because people chose one another over their belongings.
Night trouble tests the loose latch by the cauldron first. We fixed every latch before sunset.
I stayed near the tannery corner and listened for anyone calling from the dark.
Dawn gave us enough light to count wounds and missing blocks.
A zombie reached the animal pens before the bell woke us.
I pulled on one boot and ran outside carrying the other.
The moon gave just enough light to see movement beyond the farms.
We guided the children by voice because nobody wanted a lantern in the open.
A spider came over the roof while everyone watched the door.
The workshop became a shelter for anyone caught on this side of the square.
I used saddle straps to brace a shutter that would not stay closed.
No one knew how many creatures were outside until morning.
We heard arrows strike the wall long before we found the skeleton.
One guard kept the lane clear while families crossed to safety.
The animals stayed frightened until well after sunrise.
We need torches farther beyond the houses, not only along the paths.
I found claw marks on the leather hanging nearest the window.
The quiet after the attack felt less peaceful than the noise.
Tonight I am keeping my boots beside the bed.
A roof watch would have seen them before they reached the fences.
Every shadow looked alive until the sun cleared the fields.
The wind threw sand through every crack. I am still cleaning it out of the seams.
I checked the dye vats, then found two neighbors coughing behind the workshop.
Sand reached the cauldron, the hinges, and half our eyes.
A hard wind teaches a leatherworker which doors actually close.
We tied cloth across our faces before going out to find the animals.
The sky turned brown so quickly that people lost sight of their own homes.
I used wet hides to block the worst gap under the tannery door.
One drying rack blew apart and scattered straps across the square.
The grit ruined every open pot of dye.
We followed the fence by hand to reach an old villager living alone.
Nobody could hear the bell once the wind rose.
The camels knelt and refused to move until the storm weakened.
Fine sand worked inside every buckle we left uncovered.
We marked the shelter doors with bright cloth before visibility vanished.
My eyes still sting whenever the wind picks up.
Next time, everyone needs a face wrap stored near the door.
The well stayed covered. That may have saved us more trouble than we know.
We found footprints ending where the drifts had buried the path.
I have spent all morning shaking dust from finished boots.
At least the roofs held while the whole village disappeared behind sand.
The hides can soak another day. Warm hands, clear paths, and full hearths come first.
Snow piled against the doors, but everyone found shelter.
Cold works quietly. We checked on anyone who stayed quiet too long.
I cleared stiff frost from the hides and watched for tracks that stopped suddenly.
We fed every scrap of dry wood to the fires before dawn.
The path to the well vanished within an hour.
Leather straps went rigid enough to snap if bent too quickly.
We tied a rope between houses so nobody would lose the way.
A family spent the night in the tannery after their door froze shut.
The animals crowded together, so we hung hides across the open side of the pen.
I gave my thickest boots to someone searching for a missing child.
Snow pressed one roof beam low enough to make it groan.
We found the golem standing still under a white shell of ice.
Hot broth did more good than any speech could have.
The wind drove powder through walls that have stopped rain for years.
We need firewood stored in more than one building.
Everyone took turns clearing the same path as it filled again.
My fingers are still sore from thawing frozen buckles.
The sun came out, but the roads remain too deep for carts.
No one was lost. That is enough good news for one storm.
